newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait women stage protest to demand vote.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait women stage protest to demand vote.

text.p: Some 300 Kuwaiti men and women on Sunday held a rally to demand political rights for women who have to wait until the next century before they might be allowed to take part in parliamentary elections.

The activists gathered at Kuwait's lawyers society to demand women's right to run for parliament or at least vote but thousands of professional women ignored the rally and a call for a work strike on Sunday.
Tiny, conservative Kuwait -- the only Gulf Arab state with an elected assembly -- is holding on October 7 its second parliamentary elections since the 1991 Gulf War to choose 50 deputies.
Although women are over 50 percent of the 700,000 Kuwaitis they cannot vote or run for the next parliamentary elections which will take Kuwait into the next century.
"I believe in it and support it, but I don't see the wisdom behind a work strike," said a female civil servant who has been wearing a blue ribbon for weeks to demand political rights.
Activists are fighting two battles to lobby men for the right to vote while persuading more fellow women to join their move.
Kuwaiti women, the most liberal in a Moslem conservative area, run businesses, head diplomatic missions and help steer the country's oil industry.
Hind al-Idwani, one of the organisers of the rally, said the group had collected some 600 female and 400 male signatures in support of their demand.
"A good start if you take into consideration only two weeks of rallying support," she said.

Only one of the 248 parliamentary candidates attended the rally. Women were urged to accept an invitation later on Sunday to attend an election campaign by pan-Arab nationalist, left-leaning Abdullah al-Naibari.
On election day, the protesters plan to march to Bayan Palace, the government's headquarters, to stress their demand.
Kuwaiti women are not alone in their 30-year-old struggle.
Some of the Western powers which helped free Kuwait from Iraq's occupation in 1991 are privately urging the country to allow female participation in elections, diplomats said.

"If we can at least gain the right to vote in the next election (year 2000) it would be a great achievement in our region," human rights activist and journalist Wafa' Atiqi said from parliament which she covers for her publication.
The debate was revived in 1992 when Kuwait's parliament was restored but both the assembly and the government appeared reluctant to introduce the reform.
